label: Difficult Family
framing: The Bible is not a book of tidy families. Its pages are full of jealous brothers, scheming parents, and households that wound, and it tells the truth about them rather than smoothing it over, while still calling us to honor where we can and guard where we must.
cultural: In the biblical world the family was the whole structure of a person's life, so a fracture in the household was a fracture in everything, and to break with one's family was nearly unthinkable. Yet Scripture records the bitter rivalries of Jacob's house and Joseph's brothers without flinching, and Jesus, whose own family once thought him out of his mind, redrew the family line around those who do the will of God.
historical: The church has long held two truths in tension, the call to honor father and mother and the harder word that following Christ can divide a household. Augustine's mother, Monica, prayed for years for a pagan husband and a wayward son and lived to see both baptized, the Reformers honored the natural family while insisting the church is the deeper one, and pastors across the centuries have counseled both honor and the limits that honor does not erase.
application: Honor does not require pretending the harm did not happen, and it can take the form of distance held in grace rather than closeness held in pain. Forgive without necessarily restoring access, since forgiveness and trust are not the same thing. Where there is abuse, get safe and stay safe. And let the church be the family that holds you when the one you were born into cannot.

verses.text: Though my father and mother forsake me, the LORD will receive me.
verses.where: In a psalm of bold trust, David turns to urgent prayer and says that even if his father and mother forsake him, the LORD will receive him. The site's plain note says the psalm names what parents sometimes do and does not call the hurt small. To be received is to be gathered in and taken home: being received by God does not erase what a parent did, but it means you are not, in the end, unwanted.

verses.text: So when the Midianite traders passed by, his brothers pulled Joseph out of the pit and sold him for twenty shekels of silver to the Ishmaelites, who took him to Egypt.
verses.where: Joseph's brothers, jealous of their father's favorite, pull him out of a pit and sell him to traders for twenty shekels of silver. The site's note names it plainly: it is human trafficking, it is evil, and the Bible calls it a crime. Scripture's first great family story after the patriarchs is a family that sold one of its own.

verses.text: Then Saul hurled his spear at Jonathan to kill him; so Jonathan knew that his father was determined to kill David.
verses.where: When Jonathan defends David, his father Saul curses him with a vile insult to his mother and hurls a spear at his own son. Jonathan gets up from the table in fierce anger, and the next morning goes out to warn his friend. The Bible records a parent's rage turned on a child, and it shows the child leaving the room and protecting the one in danger.

verses.text: When King David heard all this, he was furious.
verses.where: After Amnon rapes his half-sister Tamar, her brother Absalom tells her to be quiet because he is her brother, and Tamar lives desolate in Absalom's house. The note says King David is furious but does nothing. Scripture tells this story without excusing anyone who stayed silent, and the harm done to Tamar was never her fault.

verses.text: When His family heard about this, they went out to take custody of Him, saying, “He is out of His mind.”
verses.where: When Jesus' family hears of the crowds, they set out to take custody of him, saying he is out of his mind. The note says most scholars take this as his family, and that Mark shows plainly that even those closest to Jesus did not yet understand him. Jesus did not go with them, and his brother James later became a leader of the church.

verses.text: For even His own brothers did not believe in Him.
verses.where: Jesus' brothers push him to go and show himself publicly, and John adds a quiet line: even his own brothers did not believe in him. The plain note says Jesus would not let anyone else set his timetable, not even his family. Jesus knew the loneliness of a family that does not understand.

verses.text: For I have come to turn ‘a man against his father, a daughter against her mother, a daughter-in-law against her mother-in-law. A man’s enemies will be the members of his own household.’
verses.where: Jesus warns that loyalty to him will divide households, using the words of Micah. The site's plain note says it is a picture of division, not a call to violence, and not a command to cut off your family: Jesus condemned those who neglected their parents. The division comes from others' response to him, and it is grieved, not sought.

verses.text: This mound is a witness, and this pillar is a witness, that I will not go past this mound to harm you, and you will not go past this mound and pillar to harm me.
verses.where: After twenty years of being cheated by his father-in-law, Jacob leaves, and the two men set up a heap of stones as a boundary neither will cross to harm the other. The plain note says these words are often read as a sweet blessing, but here they mean that two men who did not trust each other asked God to watch. Sometimes the peace that is possible is a boundary, kept, with God as witness.

verses.text: If it is possible on your part, live at peace with everyone.
verses.where: Paul tells believers to live at peace with everyone, and he adds two conditions: if it is possible, and as far as it depends on you. The site's plain note on the chapter says this never means staying in danger or keeping silent about harm. Peace takes two, and Paul does not pretend otherwise.

verses.text: Looking at those seated in a circle around Him, He said, “Here are My mother and My brothers! For whoever does the will of God is My brother and sister and mother.”
verses.where: When his mother and brothers stand outside asking for him, Jesus looks at the people sitting around him and says that whoever does the will of God is his brother and sister and mother. He did not despise his family, and later cared for his mother from the cross. He also made clear that the family of God is wider than the family of blood, and that no one in it is without kin.

misread.taken: Honor your father and mother is often used to tell someone who was harmed by a parent that they must keep visiting, stay silent, take the blame, or let the parent back into their children's lives, as if honor meant submitting to harm.
misread.says: The commandment asks for honor, and Scripture shows honor as respect, care and truthfulness. It never asks anyone to accept abuse. The site's notes on Ephesians 6 and Colossians 3 say plainly that no one may use the call to obey parents to keep a child quiet about abuse or send a child back to someone who is hurting them, and the notes on Romans 12 and Colossians 3 say that no passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger. An adult can honor a parent who hurt them by telling the truth, refusing revenge and praying for them, while keeping a safe distance.
misread.text: Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.

misread.taken: Jesus' answer to Peter, to forgive seventy-seven times, is often used to press someone hurt by their family to forgive at once, say nothing more about it, and go back to the way things were.
misread.says: The site's plain note on the chapter says forgiveness has been misused in exactly this way. Some have told people who were abused to forgive quickly, keep quiet, or go back to the person who hurt them, and that is not what the parable asks. Forgiveness lets go of revenge. It is not the same as trusting someone again, reconciling, or keeping quiet, it does not mean a crime should go unreported, and it can take a long time.
misread.text: Then Peter came to Jesus and asked, “Lord, how many times shall I forgive my brother who sins against me? Up to seven times?” Jesus answered, “I tell you, not just seven times, but seventy-seven times!

whole: If someone in your family is hurting you, or has hurt your children, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and if you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. What was done to you was not your fault, and no verse in the Bible asks you to stay where you or your children are in danger. Difficult family comes in many forms. For some it is cruelty, control or abuse. For others it is a parent who was never there, a brother who always took, a mother who can only criticize, or a family that has made one person carry the blame for everyone. Holidays come around and bring the dread with them. Christians in hard families often carry an extra weight: the sense that a godly person should be able to make it work, and that the commandment to honor their parents means they must keep enduring it.

Scripture is not a book of tidy families, and it does not pretend to be. Joseph's brothers sold him. Saul hurled a spear at his own son. When Tamar was raped by her half-brother, her other brother told her to be quiet and her father did nothing. Jesus' own family thought he was out of his mind and his brothers did not believe him. The Bible tells these stories plainly and does not call any of the harm good. It also names the causes beneath much family pain: favoritism, envy, unconfessed sin passed down a generation, and silence that protects the one doing harm instead of the one being harmed. Many of us have been part of that silence somewhere, and seeing it is the start of refusing it.

So the Bible's wisdom here is honor without pretense. Honor what can be honored, and tell the truth about what cannot. Where a family member is safe and willing, seek peace as far as it depends on you, which Paul admits is not always far. Where they are not, a boundary can be the most honest peace there is; Jacob and Laban set up stones and asked God to watch. Forgiveness lets go of revenge and leaves judgment to God, but it does not require trust, contact or silence, and it may take a long time. Report crimes to the authorities. Protect children first. Get help from a pastor or counselor who understands families like yours. And let the church be what Jesus said it is, a family wider than blood, where no one is without kin.

The hope Scripture gives is not that every family will be healed in this life, though some are, slowly. Joseph's brothers did come to him years later, and there were tears. It is that the God who receives those whom father and mother forsake does not lose track of anyone his family failed. Jesus knew what it was to be misunderstood by his own, and he made a new family out of everyone who does his Father's will. You may need to grieve the family you did not have. You do not have to do it alone, and you are not, in the end, unwanted.
deep.sit: Is there a peace you have been told you must make that is not yours to make alone, and what would a safe and honest boundary look like instead?

prayer.lead: The end of the psalm that says the LORD will receive those whom father and mother forsake. Pray it slowly, and wait.
prayer.text: Still I am certain to see the goodness of the LORD in the land of the living. Wait patiently for the LORD; be strong and courageous. Wait patiently for the LORD!

careLines.text: If you are being hurt in some other place, at home, at work or in a church, the same is true.
Tell someone you trust and get help.
Nothing in this passage asks anyone to stay where they or their children are in danger.
What was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault.
If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
